name: Toxicity Forecasting
title: Toxicity Forecasting
answer: Toxicity forecasting is the use of computational models to predict whether a chemical or drug candidate will cause harm to the liver, heart, kidney, or other organs before it is tested in animals or people. It sits inside drug discovery and molecular simulation, where it screens large libraries of compounds and flags likely problems early. The work covers endpoints such as hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, mutagenicity, and general cytotoxicity, and it draws on assay data, chemical structure, and increasingly on gene expression and imaging readouts.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Toxicity forecasting is the use of computational models to predict whether a chemical or drug candidate will cause harm to the liver, heart, kidney, or other organs before it is tested in animals or people. It sits inside drug discovery and molecular simulation, where it screens large libraries of compounds and flags likely problems early. The work covers endpoints such as hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, mutagenicity, and general cytotoxicity, and it draws on assay data, chemical structure, and increasingly on gene expression and imaging readouts.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models run on standard research computing, typically Linux servers with graphics processing units for the deep learning parts and ordinary clusters for the rest. The data comes from public sources such as Tox21, ToxCast, and ChEMBL, from internal pharmaceutical assay archives, and from chemical databases that supply molecular structures. Common toolkits include RDKit for handling molecules, PyTorch or TensorFlow for the models, and graph neural network libraries for structure based prediction. Cloud compute is often used when a screen covers millions of compounds.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical project starts by assembling a labelled set of compounds with known toxicity outcomes, then featurising each molecule as fingerprints, descriptors, or a molecular graph. Models range from simple regression and random forests to graph neural networks and, more recently, pretrained chemical language models. Because toxic outcomes are rare, class imbalance, scaffold splits, and applicability domain checks matter more than raw accuracy. Predictions are validated against held out chemical series and, where possible, against experimental assays before they influence a project decision.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Toxicity predictions inform safety decisions but do not replace regulatory toxicology studies, and agencies such as the FDA and EMA expect documented validation and defined domains of use. Provenance of training data, model version, and the exact endpoint predicted all need to be recorded so a result can be reproduced and defended. Where a model contributes to a regulatory submission, guidance such as OECD principles for validated QSAR models and ICH safety guidelines shape what evidence is acceptable. This site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which is a reminder that safety claims carry legal weight. Nothing here is legal or medical advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward models that combine structure, assay, and omics data, and toward foundation models pretrained on large chemical and biological corpora and then fine tuned for specific toxicity endpoints. Organ on a chip and human cell based assays are generating new training data that may reduce reliance on animal studies. Regulators are also exploring how to accept computational evidence more formally, which would raise the bar on validation and documentation. Expect more emphasis on uncertainty estimates and on models that explain which part of a molecule drives a predicted risk.
